title: Regional Cooperation
tagline: ASEAN, the European Union, SAARC, BRICS and QUAD — their aims and economic achievements.

overview.intro: Regional cooperation is the arrangement by which neighbouring states coordinate policy to gain what acting alone cannot secure. This unit examines five contrasting organisations — ASEAN, the European Union, SAARC, BRICS and the QUAD — their aims, their methods and their economic achievements, so that a student can compare a deep union, an economic bloc, a neighbourhood forum, a grouping of large emerging economies and a loose strategic consultation.

facts.label: EU
facts.value: The deepest integration: customs union, single market, the euro in the member states, and shared institutions with binding law.

facts.label: ASEAN
facts.value: Founded 1967; economic growth and centrality in regional architecture, on the principle of non-interference and consensus.

facts.label: SAARC
facts.value: Founded 1985; South Asian cooperation constrained by bilateral disputes, with the SAFTA free trade area as its main economic instrument.

facts.label: BRICS and QUAD
facts.value: BRICS: large emerging economies coordinating on finance and reform of institutions. QUAD: India, USA, Japan, Australia consulting on Indo-Pacific security and standards.

learningOutcomes: Explain why states engage in regional cooperation.
Describe the aims and achievements of the EU and ASEAN.
Assess SAARC’s record in South Asia.
Explain the purpose of BRICS and the QUAD.
Compare the levels of integration achieved by these groupings.

blocks.text: The arguments for regional cooperation are of three kinds. The economic argument is that neighbouring states trade heavily with one another, so removing tariffs and aligning standards enlarges the market for all of them, allows specialisation and attracts investment that a small isolated market cannot. The security argument is that states which bind their economies together and consult regularly have less reason to fight and more capacity to manage disputes, a logic visible in the European project’s origin in the coal and steel pool of rivals. The political argument is that a regional bloc carries weight in negotiations with larger powers that its members could not command separately.

Against these stand the familiar objections. Cooperation constrains policy autonomy: a customs union surrenders independent trade policy, and a monetary union surrenders independent monetary policy. Benefits are unevenly distributed within the grouping, which creates losers who become political opponents of the arrangement. And regionalism can become exclusive, dividing the region from the rest of the world rather than integrating it. Each of the organisations in this unit represents a different answer to how much autonomy a state should surrender and for what return.

blocks.text: The European Union is the deepest form of regional cooperation in existence. It began as the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951, pooling the industries of former enemies so that war became materially difficult, and developed through the European Economic Community into a union with a customs union, a single market without internal border checks, a common trade policy and a single currency used by most members. Its institutions — a directly elected parliament, a commission, a council and a court whose law takes precedence in its fields — give it something close to federal character, and its economic achievement is substantial: the world’s largest single market, deep supply-chain integration, and a common regulatory standard that firms worldwide must meet to sell into it. Its limits are equally instructive, since decision-making by unanimity among member governments has repeatedly slowed responses to crisis, and the departure of a member demonstrated that the union is reversible in a way its founders did not contemplate.

ASEAN, founded in 1967, follows the opposite model. It proceeds by consensus and non-interference in internal affairs, has no parliament and no supranational court, and binds its members loosely while dealing with them diplomatically. Its achievement is different in kind: it has kept the peace among its members through the habit of consultation, it has become the hub of East Asian regional architecture through forums that include the great powers, and its economies have grown rapidly with trade among members rising steeply and attracting investment through integrated supply chains. Its weakness is the mirror image of its principle: disputes in the South China Sea and differences among members over how to respond to them have shown that consensus can produce statements too mild to constrain anyone, which is the cost of choosing sovereignty over institution.

blocks.text: SAARC was founded in 1985 by the seven states of South Asia to accelerate economic growth, social progress and cultural development among them. Its achievement has been modest: the South Asian Free Trade Area came into force well behind schedule, non-tariff barriers remain high, and cooperation has repeatedly been suspended by bilateral conflict, since the charter excludes bilateral and contentious issues from the forum. Its durable contributions are the sectoral conventions — on mutual legal assistance, on terrorism, on the grid and the highway — and the habit of meeting at all, but the record explains why the region’s trade share with itself remains low compared with East Asia or Europe.

BRICS brings together large emerging economies for a different purpose: to press for reform of the international financial institutions, where voting shares had long failed to reflect their weight, to develop cooperative finance through a new development bank, and to coordinate positions on trade and monetary questions. Its economic weight is genuine — together its members hold a large share of population, output and reserves — and its practical achievement lies in creating an alternative channel of coordination outside the traditional institutions, though its members differ widely in political system and strategic alignment, which limits how far it can act as a bloc.

The QUAD brings together India, the United States, Japan and Australia in a consultation focused on the Indo-Pacific. It is not a treaty alliance and establishes no permanent secretariat: its cooperation runs through summits, working groups and practical programmes — vaccines supplied jointly, maritime domain awareness, critical-technology standards and infrastructure finance offered as an alternative to single-source lending. Its significance lies partly in what it is not: having begun informally and been suspended once, it has survived precisely because it demands no sovereignty from its members and can therefore accommodate partners who will not join a formal bloc.

Its limits follow from the same design. Without a charter there is no obligation to act collectively, members retain divergent relationships with major powers, and the grouping cannot announce positions its members will not take individually. Supporters answer that this is a feature rather than a defect: in a region where formal alliances are contested, a flexible forum can build habits of cooperation and deliver concrete projects without provoking the resistance that a treaty would. The honest assessment is that the QUAD tests whether cooperation can be built on shared interest and shared standards rather than on shared obligations — which is the same question the other groupings answer differently.

blocks.text: Placed side by side the five groupings show a spectrum rather than a hierarchy. At one end the European Union surrenders substantial sovereignty to gain market depth, standard-setting power and a collective political voice; in the middle ASEAN and SAARC retain full sovereignty and gain consultation, peace among members and a seat at regional tables; at the other end BRICS and the QUAD are not regional organisations in the traditional sense at all but coalitions of convenience that coordinate around a specific purpose — institutional reform in one case, regional order in the other — without surrendering anything.

The comparison also shows that depth and durability are not the same. The EU is deep but contested by its own members; ASEAN is shallow but has held its members together through decades of rapid change; SAARC is constrained by the disputes that make cooperation most needed; and the newest groupings will be judged by whether their coordination survives the disagreements that are certain to arise. The exam answer that earns the highest marks names the level of integration each has chosen, identifies what was surrendered to achieve it, and judges whether the exchange was worth making — which is the same question in every case.

items: Deeper integration buys depth of market and standard-setting power at the cost of autonomy.
Consensus models preserve sovereignty but struggle to act decisively.
Trade within a region is the clearest economic indicator of cooperation’s success.
Sectoral cooperation — energy, legal assistance, infrastructure — often advances where political cooperation stalls.
The right comparison is not which is best but which exchange each grouping chose.

keyPoints: Regional cooperation rests on economic, security and political arguments.
Its cost is policy autonomy, uneven gains and the risk of exclusivity.
The EU grew from the coal and steel pool of 1951 into a union with a single market and currency.
EU institutions give it near-federal character with law that takes precedence in its fields.
ASEAN proceeds by consensus and non-interference and has kept the peace among members.
SAARC was founded in 1985; SAFTA and sectoral conventions are its main achievements.
Bilateral disputes repeatedly constrain SAARC’s cooperation.
BRICS coordinates to reform international institutions and develop cooperative finance.
The QUAD consults on Indo-Pacific security, standards and infrastructure.
Each grouping represents a different choice about how much sovereignty to surrender.

questions.prompt: The free trade area that came into force among the SAARC member states is SAFTA — the South Asian Free Trade __________ .
questions.explanation: Its schedule of tariff reduction ran behind the original timetable, and non-tariff barriers remain high.

questions.prompt: The grouping of India, the United States, Japan and Australia that consults on the Indo-Pacific is the __________ .
questions.explanation: It coordinates on security, infrastructure and standards without establishing a treaty organisation.

questions.prompt: State four arguments in favour of regional cooperation.
questions.answer: Four arguments are: larger markets, which allow specialisation, economies of scale and investment that a small isolated market cannot attract; reduced likelihood of conflict, since states that bind their economies together and consult regularly have less reason to fight; greater weight in global negotiations, because a bloc can bargain where a small state cannot; and coordination of standards and infrastructure that neighbours share. The post-war peace in Europe, built on the pooling of coal and steel, is also accepted as evidence.
questions.explanation: Each argument must state the mechanism, not merely assert benefit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the European Union and ASEAN as models of regional cooperation.
questions.answer: The European Union is a supranational model: it was built from the coal and steel pool of 1951, developed a customs union and a single market with free movement of goods, services, capital and people, adopted a common currency in most member states, and possesses institutions — a directly elected parliament, a commission, a council and a court whose law takes precedence — that exercise authority above the national governments. ASEAN is an intergovernmental model: founded in 1967, it proceeds by consensus and non-interference, has no parliament or supranational court, and binds members loosely through consultation. The contrast shows a trade-off — the EU gains depth of market and standard-setting power but surrenders autonomy and is slowed by unanimity, while ASEAN preserves sovereignty fully but has produced soft responses to disputes such as those in the South China Sea. Both have kept the peace among their members, but through entirely different means.
questions.explanation: The answer must compare on method, economic depth and political form, and draw the trade-off explicitly.

questions.prompt: Assess the aims and economic achievements of regional cooperation with reference to ASEAN, SAARC and BRICS.
questions.answer: The three groupings pursue different aims through different instruments, and their records diverge accordingly. ASEAN’s aims from its founding in 1967 were to accelerate economic growth, social progress and cultural development and to maintain peace in the region through consultation, and its method has been consensus and non-interference. Its economic achievement is considerable: intraregional trade rose steeply over the decades, member economies became integrated into common supply chains in electronics and manufacturing, investment was attracted by the size and stability of the grouping, and ASEAN became the hub of East Asian architecture through forums that draw in the great powers. Its limitation is that consensus has produced mild responses to the South China Sea disputes, where members take different positions. SAARC, founded in 1985 by the seven states of South Asia, aimed at the same growth and social progress but has a modest record: the South Asian Free Trade Area came into force behind schedule, non-tariff barriers remain high, the region’s share of trade with itself stays low compared with East Asia or Europe, and bilateral conflict has repeatedly displaced the cooperative agenda because the charter excludes contentious issues. Its achievements lie in sectoral conventions on legal assistance, terrorism, energy grids and highways rather than in trade. BRICS is a different kind of body altogether: a coordination of large emerging economies seeking reform of the international financial institutions, where voting shares failed to reflect their weight, and the creation of cooperative finance through a development bank, with a genuine share of world population, output and reserves behind its demands. The assessment turns on aims: ASEAN has delivered peace and integration at the cost of mildness, SAARC has delivered consultation where the political conditions allow little more, and BRICS has delivered an alternative channel of coordination without claiming integration at all. Marks come from judging each against the aims it actually set rather than against a single standard.
questions.explanation: Full marks need each grouping with its aim, method and concrete achievement, then a judgement applying each grouping’s own standard.

questions.prompt: Does deeper regional integration produce better outcomes than loose cooperation? Discuss with reference to the European Union and ASEAN.
questions.answer: The case for depth rests on what the European Union has achieved that ASEAN cannot. A customs union and single market eliminate not only tariffs but the border checks, differing standards and regulatory arbitrage that limit trade, so firms plan continental supply chains and consumers gain from a market of hundreds of millions; common external tariffs give the union bargaining weight in trade negotiations that no member would have alone; the euro removes exchange risk within its area; and legal precedence for union law means commitments are enforceable rather than aspirational. By these measures depth converts sovereignty into measurable economic and political capacity. The case for loose cooperation is equally concrete. ASEAN’s consensus and non-interference preserved the peace among members who had fought each other within living memory, admitted new members without disruption, and made it possible for states at very different levels of development and different political systems to cooperate at all — something a supranational model could not have managed in Southeast Asia. Its flexibility also allowed rapid adaptation: the ASEAN free trade area advanced, supply chains integrated regardless of treaty depth, and the grouping became the centre of regional forums precisely because it did not demand political concessions. The EU’s difficulties display the costs of depth: unanimity has slowed responses to crisis, economic divergence between members has produced strains that suspension of fiscal rules could not resolve, migration and sovereignty disputes have driven a member to leave, and public support for further integration is uneven. The strongest conclusion distinguishes the conditions under which each works: depth pays where members share a high degree of trust, comparable institutions and a compelling security reason to bind together, as in post-war Europe, and it fails or provokes backlash where those conditions are absent; loose cooperation delivers less but absorbs disagreement, which is why ASEAN has proved durable across a diversity the EU could not have accommodated. A strong essay therefore judges by conditions and by which outcomes — trade, peace, resilience, legitimacy — are being weighed, rather than treating depth as good in itself.
questions.explanation: Full marks require specific achievements and failures on both sides, an explicit statement of the conditions under which each model works, and a reasoned judgement that ties the verdict to which outcomes matter.
